---
title: "A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Levels of organisation

### 1.1

Arrange from the smallest to the largest level: organ, organism, cell,
organ system, tissue.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
:::

### 1.2

In a multicellular animal, most cells exchange materials directly with:

a. the external environment
b. interstitial fluid
c. blood plasma
d. the gut lumen

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b. Interstitial (extracellular) fluid surrounds the cells; blood, where present,
transports material between exchange organs and the tissues.
:::

### 1.3

The intestinal wall contains all four primary tissue types. For each tissue
type, give its main function in the intestine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Tissue | Function in the intestine |
| --- | --- |
| Epithelium | Lines the lumen; secretion and absorption |
| Connective tissue | Supports the epithelium and carries blood vessels |
| Smooth muscle | Mixes and moves the contents |
| Nervous tissue | Coordinates secretion and muscle activity |
:::

### 1.4

Put the steps in order for a glucose molecule moving from the gut lumen into
a skeletal-muscle cell:

a. crosses the muscle-cell membrane
b. crosses the apical membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
c. is carried in the blood
d. crosses the basolateral membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
e. enters the interstitial fluid around the muscle fibre

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → c → e → a. Glucose in the lumen has not yet been absorbed, because the
lumen is continuous with the outside of the body.
:::

## Surface area, volume and diffusion

### 2.1

Complete the table for cubes with side length $L$.

| $L$ (mm) | Surface area (mm²) | Volume (mm³) | Surface area : volume (mm⁻¹) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | | | |
| 2 | | | |
| 4 | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| $L$ (mm) | Surface area (mm²) | Volume (mm³) | Surface area : volume (mm⁻¹) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 6 | 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 24 | 8 | 3 |
| 4 | 96 | 64 | 1.5 |

The ratio is $6L^2 / L^3 = 6/L$, so each doubling of $L$ halves it.
:::

### 2.2

The time needed for diffusion is proportional to the square of the distance.
By what factor does the diffusion time change when the distance increases
from:

a. 1 µm to 3 µm
b. 0.1 mm to 1 mm
c. 20 µm to 10 µm

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 3² = 9 times longer.
b. 10² = 100 times longer.
c. (1/2)² = 1/4, i.e. four times shorter.
:::

### 2.3

Name three ways in which large animals overcome the low surface-area-to-volume
ratio of a large body.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. Folding, branching or subdivision of exchange surfaces increases the area
   (e.g. alveoli, gill lamellae, intestinal villi).
2. Thin exchange barriers shorten the diffusion distance.
3. Bulk flow (ventilation and circulation) moves material over long distances.
:::

## Tissues

### 3.1

Name the primary tissue type that matches each description.

| | Description |
| --- | --- |
| A | One layer of closely packed cells lining a lumen, with little material between the cells |
| B | Widely spaced cells among abundant parallel extracellular fibres |
| C | Long, cylindrical, striated fibres with many nuclei per fibre |
| D | Cells with long processes, surrounded by many smaller supporting cells |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

A: epithelial tissue (simple epithelium). B: connective tissue (dense regular
connective tissue, e.g. tendon). C: muscle tissue (skeletal muscle).
D: nervous tissue (neurons and glial cells).
:::

### 3.2

Complete the table.

| | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle | Smooth muscle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Striated? | | | |
| Cell shape | | | |
| Nuclei per cell | | | |
| Specialised cell junctions | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle | Smooth muscle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Striated? | Yes | Yes | No |
| Cell shape | Long cylindrical fibres | Branched cells | Spindle-shaped cells |
| Nuclei per cell | Many | One (sometimes two) | One |
| Specialised cell junctions | No | Intercalated discs | Gap junctions in many smooth muscles |
:::

### 3.3

Which type of epithelium best suits each function: simple squamous or
stratified squamous?

a. gas exchange
b. protection against abrasion

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Simple squamous: a single thin layer gives a short diffusion distance.
b. Stratified squamous: several cell layers protect the tissue beneath.
:::

### 3.4

Define the terms *lumen*, *apical surface* and *basal surface*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Lumen:** the inner space of a tube or cavity, such as the gut or a blood vessel.
- **Apical surface:** the side of an epithelial cell that faces the lumen or
  the outside.
- **Basal surface:** the side of an epithelial cell that faces the basement
  membrane and underlying tissue.
:::

### 3.5

A section shows a circular profile with an empty centre. Why is this not
enough to identify it as a blood vessel?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Any tube (such as a duct, gland, gut or vessel) cut in cross-section gives a
ring. An oblique cut through the same tube gives an oval. Identification also
needs the wall structure, its tissue layers and the scale.
:::

## Homeostasis and feedback

### 4.1

Define homeostasis.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Homeostasis is the active maintenance of internal conditions (such as
temperature or the composition of extracellular fluid) within a range
compatible with life, despite external and internal disturbances.
:::

### 4.2

Body temperature in a mammal rises during exercise. Match each item to its
role in the feedback loop: regulated variable, sensor, control centre, effector.

a. sweat glands
b. hypothalamus
c. body temperature
d. thermoreceptors

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. effector; b. control centre; c. regulated variable; d. sensor.
:::

### 4.3

State whether each example is negative or positive feedback.

a. A rise in blood glucose increases insulin secretion, which lowers blood glucose.
b. Uterine contractions increase oxytocin release, which strengthens the contractions.
c. A rise in body temperature increases sweating.
d. Activated clotting factors activate more clotting factors.
e. A fall in blood pressure increases heart rate through the baroreceptor reflex.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Negative. b. Positive. c. Negative. d. Positive. e. Negative.
:::

### 4.4

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Positive feedback means that the response is good for the animal.
b. In negative feedback, the response reduces the deviation that triggered it.
c. Positive feedback must have a way to stop.
d. A stable internal concentration means that no transport is taking place.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. "Positive" refers to the direction of the loop: the response
   amplifies the original change. It says nothing about benefit.
b. True.
c. True. Otherwise the change keeps growing, as in an action potential or
   during birth.
d. False. Inputs and outputs can balance while transport continues.
:::

## Responses, acclimation and adaptation

### 5.1

Classify each example as an acute response, acclimation or evolutionary
adaptation.

a. Ventilation increases within seconds when an animal starts running.
b. A fish kept at a higher temperature for four weeks changes its enzyme levels.
c. A population of fish living in hypoxic water has inherited larger gill surfaces.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Acute response. b. Acclimation. c. Evolutionary adaptation.
:::

### 5.2

What is the difference between *acclimation* and *acclimatisation*?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Both are reversible changes within one individual. Acclimation describes the
response to a change in one condition, usually in the laboratory.
Acclimatisation describes the response to changes in the natural environment.
:::

### 5.3

Complete the table comparing oxygen delivery to the tissues.

| | Insect | Mammal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | | |
| Exchange surface | | |
| Route from exchange surface to the tissue cells | | |
| Role of the circulatory system in O₂ transport | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Insect | Mammal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | Air | Air |
| Exchange surface | Tracheoles, the fine endings of the tracheae, at the tissues | Alveoli in the lungs |
| Route from exchange surface to the tissue cells | Air-filled tracheae branch directly to the tissues | Blood carries O₂, mostly bound to haemoglobin, from lungs to tissues |
| Role of the circulatory system in O₂ transport | Small | Essential |
:::

## Explore: Diffusion limits body size {#explore-a1-scaling}

The demo shows a ball (or flat sheet) of tissue in air-saturated water that
gets O₂ only by diffusion from its surface. Colour shows the O₂ level and the
readouts give A/V, the diffusion time to the centre, the largest size that
diffusion can supply and the O₂ at the centre. Use the radius and O₂-use
sliders, or the preset buttons.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a1-scaling"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a1-scaling.js"></script>
```

### E1

Press **Reset** (sphere, radius 0.50 mm, O₂ use 0.20 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹). Read off:

a. A/V
b. the diffusion time to the centre
c. the O₂ at the centre, as % of the surface value

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 6.00 mm⁻¹ (= 3/r for a sphere).
b. About 62 s ($t \approx x^2/2D$ with $x$ = 0.5 mm and $D$ = 2 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹).
c. 81 %. Every cell gets O₂.
:::

### E2

From Reset, drag the radius up to 1.0 mm.

a. By what factor has A/V changed?
b. By what factor has the diffusion time to the centre changed?
c. What does the readout give as the largest radius that diffusion alone can
   supply?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. It halves, from 6.00 to 3.00 mm⁻¹ (A/V ∝ 1/r).
b. It increases four times, from about 62 s to 250 s (shown as 4 min),
   because diffusion time ∝ r².
c. 1.14 mm. Above this radius an anoxic core appears; at 1.0 mm the centre
   still has about 23 % O₂.
:::

### E3

Press **5 mm ball**. What percentage of the tissue gets no O₂?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

About 64 %. The radius is more than four times the largest radius (1.14 mm)
that diffusion can supply, so most of the volume is anoxic.
:::

### E4

Press **Mouse tissue** (radius 0.50 mm, O₂ use 2.5 mL g⁻¹ h⁻¹, about 12 times
the Reset value).

a. What is now the largest radius that diffusion can supply?
b. Which statement explains the change? (i) the largest radius falls in
   proportion to the O₂ use; (ii) the largest radius falls in proportion to
   the square root of the O₂ use; (iii) the largest radius does not depend
   on the O₂ use.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 323 µm (0.32 mm), so the 0.50 mm ball now has an anoxic core (17 % of the
   tissue).
b. (ii). The largest radius is $\sqrt{6DC_0/M}$; 12.5 times the O₂ use gives
   $\sqrt{12.5} \approx 3.5$ times smaller radius (1.14 mm → 0.32 mm). A
   tissue with a mammalian metabolic rate must therefore be supplied over much
   shorter distances, by capillaries.
:::

### E5

Press **Flatworm** (flat sheet, 0.15 mm half-thickness).

a. What is the largest half-thickness that diffusion can supply?
b. Does this limit depend on the length and width of the sheet?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 660 µm (0.66 mm), i.e. a sheet up to about 1.3 mm thick. For a flat sheet
   the limit is $\sqrt{2DC_0/M}$, which is $1/\sqrt{3}$ of the sphere's limit.
b. No. Only the thickness sets the diffusion distance, so a flatworm can be
   several centimetres long and wide as long as it stays thin.
:::

## Explore: Feedback control of body temperature {#explore-a1-feedback}

The demo simulates body temperature under a heat load from exercise (or cold)
between minute 10 and minute 40. The effector response is proportional to the
deviation from the 37 °C set point. Choose the type of loop with the buttons,
set the gain, response delay and disturbance with the sliders, and read the
deviations in the readout.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a1-feedback"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a1-feedback.js"></script>
```

### E6

Press **Reset** (negative feedback, gain 0.5, no delay, disturbance
+0.30 °C min⁻¹).

a. What is the deviation from the set point at minute 40?
b. Is the temperature back at 37 ± 0.1 °C at 60 min?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. +0.55 °C. Some deviation remains during the whole exercise period, because
   the effector response is driven by the deviation itself.
b. Yes.
:::

### E7

Keep negative feedback and set the gain to 1.0, then to 2.0 (**Strong, fast**).
Read the deviation at minute 40 each time. What happens to the remaining
error when the gain is doubled?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Gain 1.0: +0.29 °C. Gain 2.0: +0.15 °C. Doubling the gain roughly halves the
remaining error; a stronger response holds the regulated variable closer to
the set point, but never exactly on it.
:::

### E8

Return to **Reset** and press **None**, then **Positive feedback**. For each,
read the deviation at minute 40 and say whether the temperature is back at
37 °C by 60 min.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Loop | Deviation at minute 40 | Back at 37 °C at 60 min? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| None | +4.66 °C | No |
| Positive feedback | +13.00 °C (runs off the top of the plot) | No |

Without feedback the heat load drives a drift of several degrees. With
positive feedback the response amplifies the deviation, so temperature runs
away out of the survivable range and does not return when exercise stops.
:::

### E9

Press **Strong, slow** (gain 2.0, delay 1.5 min). Then lower the gain to 0.5
while keeping the 1.5 min delay.

a. What happens with gain 2.0 and the delay?
b. What is the largest deviation with gain 0.5 and the delay?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. The temperature overshoots the set point and oscillates with growing
   amplitude until it leaves the survivable range: a strong response that
   acts on old information over-corrects.
b. +0.69 °C (compared with +0.55 °C without delay). With a weaker response
   the delay causes only a small overshoot, and temperature returns to 37 °C.
:::

### E10

Press **Cold** (disturbance −0.30 °C min⁻¹). What is the deviation at minute
40, and is the effector cooling or heating the body?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

−0.55 °C, the mirror image of Reset. The effector trace lies below the line:
it is heating (for example shivering), opposing the fall in temperature.
:::

## Bioinformatics and R {#bioinformatics}

These exercises use **UniProtKB**, the main database of protein sequences and
their functions, together with R. Each exercise is a separate small problem
about how body size and tissue organisation show up in real data. Run the R code
in R or RStudio; only base R and the MASS package (installed with every copy of
R) are used. The code reads sequences directly from the internet, so you need a
network connection.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to search UniProtKB

Go to <https://www.uniprot.org> and type a query in the search box. Plain words
(`myoglobin`) search every field, which gives many unwanted hits. Field queries
are more precise and can be combined with `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`:

| Query | Finds |
|---|---|
| `gene:MB` | entries whose gene name or gene-name synonym is MB |
| `protein_name:myoglobin` | entries with "myoglobin" in the protein name |
| `organism_id:9606` | human (NCBI taxonomy number); mouse is `10090` |
| `organism_name:"sperm whale"` | organisms whose name contains the phrase |
| `reviewed:true` | only **Swiss-Prot** entries, curated by experts |

Example: `gene:MB AND organism_id:9606 AND reviewed:true`.

**Reviewed** (Swiss-Prot, gold star icon) entries are checked by curators and
there is normally one per protein and species. **Unreviewed** (TrEMBL) entries
are computer-annotated and often fragments or duplicates. Use the
*Reviewed* filter in the left-hand panel, or add `reviewed:true`.

Each entry has a stable **accession** (for example `P02144`) and an entry
name (`MYG_HUMAN`). Cite the accession: it does not change between releases.
An entry page is divided into sections: *Function*, *Names & Taxonomy*,
*Subcellular Location*, *PTM/Processing* (with the *Features* table giving
positions such as the mature chain), *Family & Domains* and *Sequence*.
The sequence in FASTA format is at
`https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/<accession>.fasta`; R can read that address
with `readLines()`.
:::

### B1. Finding the right myoglobin

Myoglobin is the oxygen-binding protein of muscle. You want the myoglobin of
three mammals that differ about a million-fold in body mass: mouse, human and
sperm whale. Use UniProtKB.

a. Search `gene:MB AND organism_id:9606`. Many hits appear, most of them short.
   Tick the *Reviewed* filter. What is the accession of the reviewed human
   myoglobin entry?
b. Search `gene:MB AND organism_id:10090 AND reviewed:true` (mouse). The
   reviewed list contains more than myoglobin, for example the B-cell protein
   CD79A. Why?
   1. CD79A is a myoglobin that is expressed in blood cells
   2. `gene:` also matches gene-name synonyms, and CD79A has the old synonym
      Mb-1
   3. The search ignores the organism filter
   4. Unreviewed entries were not removed
c. Search `myoglobin AND organism_name:"sperm whale" AND reviewed:true`. Three
   reviewed entries appear, from three different whale species. Which accession
   belongs to the sperm whale, *Physeter macrocephalus* (taxonomy number 9755)?
   Which query would have given only this entry?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. **P02144** (entry name MYG_HUMAN, 154 amino acids). The unreviewed hits are
   mostly automatically predicted fragments from alternative transcripts.
b. **2.** Field `gene:` searches gene names *and* their synonyms. Always check
   the protein name and organism of a hit, not only that it matched.
c. **P02185** (MYG_PHYMC). The others are the dwarf (*Kogia sima*, P02184) and
   pygmy sperm whale (*Kogia breviceps*, Q0KIY5), whose common names also
   contain "sperm whale". `gene:MB AND organism_id:9755 AND reviewed:true`
   (or `protein_name:myoglobin AND organism_id:9755`) gives only P02185: a
   taxonomy number is unambiguous where a common name is not.
:::

### B2. What does myoglobin do in a muscle fibre?

Open the human myoglobin entry, <https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P02144/entry>.

a. In the *Function* section, myoglobin's primary function is to store oxygen
   and to … (choose one)
   1. carry oxygen in blood plasma between lungs and tissues
   2. facilitate the diffusion of oxygen within muscle tissue
   3. pump oxygen across the plasma membrane
b. In *Subcellular Location*, where in the cell is myoglobin found?
c. In the *Features* table (section *PTM/Processing*) the chain "Myoglobin"
   runs from position 2 to 154. How many amino acids does the mature protein
   have, and what happened to residue 1?
d. In the *Function* section's features, which amino acid is at position 94
   (the proximal residue binding heme), and what does it hold in place?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. **2.** Myoglobin stores O₂ and speeds its movement from the capillary side
   of a muscle fibre to the mitochondria, which helps with the diffusion limit
   over distances of tens of micrometres discussed in this unit.
b. In the **cytoplasm of the muscle cell, the sarcoplasm**. Unlike haemoglobin
   it is not in blood: it works inside the tissue, on the last part of the
   oxygen path.
c. **153 amino acids.** The initiator methionine (residue 1) is removed after
   translation, which is why the mature chain starts at position 2.
d. **Histidine (H94)**. It binds the iron of the **heme** group; oxygen binds
   on the other side of the heme, near another histidine at position 65.
:::

### B3. Is a whale's myoglobin a scaled-up mouse myoglobin?

A sperm whale is roughly a million times heavier than a mouse. Do its muscle
proteins also differ in size? Read the three FASTA files from B1 into R and
compare them. All three proteins have the same length, so the residues can be
compared position by position without an alignment program.

```r
read_uniprot <- function(acc) {
  url   <- paste0("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/", acc, ".fasta")
  lines <- readLines(url)
  cat(lines[1], "\n")                      # the header line
  paste(lines[-1], collapse = "")          # join the sequence lines
}
human <- read_uniprot("P02144")
mouse <- read_uniprot("P04247")
whale <- read_uniprot("P02185")
nchar(c(human = human, mouse = mouse, whale = whale))

h <- strsplit(human, "")[[1]]              # one letter per residue
m <- strsplit(mouse, "")[[1]]
w <- strsplit(whale, "")[[1]]
identity <- function(a, b) round(100 * mean(a == b), 1)   # % identical positions
c(human_mouse = identity(h, m),
  human_whale = identity(h, w),
  mouse_whale = identity(m, w))
sum(h == m & h == w)                       # positions identical in all three
c(human = h[c(65, 94)], mouse = m[c(65, 94)], whale = w[c(65, 94)])
```

a. How long is myoglobin in each species?
b. Which pair of species is the least similar, and what is its percentage
   identity?
c. At how many of the positions are all three species identical?
d. Are the two oxygen- and heme-binding histidines (positions 65 and 94)
   conserved in all three?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
>sp|P02144|MYG_HUMAN Myoglobin OS=Homo sapiens OX=9606 GN=MB PE=1 SV=2 
>sp|P04247|MYG_MOUSE Myoglobin OS=Mus musculus OX=10090 GN=Mb PE=1 SV=3 
>sp|P02185|MYG_PHYMC Myoglobin OS=Physeter macrocephalus OX=9755 GN=MB PE=1 SV=2 
human mouse whale 
  154   154   154 
human_mouse human_whale mouse_whale 
       83.8        84.4        79.9 
[1] 118
human1 human2 mouse1 mouse2 whale1 whale2 
   "H"    "H"    "H"    "H"    "H"    "H" 
```

a. **154 amino acids** in all three.
b. **Mouse and sperm whale, 79.9 %.** Human is about equally close to both
   (about 84 %).
c. **118** of 154 positions.
d. **Yes**, both histidines are present in all three.

Body size scales organs, not molecules. A protein that does one job (holding
oxygen on a heme) keeps its size and its key residues across a million-fold
range of body mass. Large divers differ instead in how *much* myoglobin their
muscles contain and in some surface residues.
:::

### B4. Do big mammals have proportionally big brains?

`MASS::mammals` holds real average body mass (kg) and brain mass (g) of 62
mammal species. If brain mass were proportional to body mass, the slope of
log(brain) against log(body) would be 1. A slope of 2/3 would match the
surface-area rule used in this unit.

```r
library(MASS)                     # ships with R
head(mammals)
fit <- lm(log10(brain) ~ log10(body), data = mammals)
round(coef(fit), 3)
round(confint(fit), 3)           # 95 % confidence intervals
plot(log10(mammals$body), log10(mammals$brain),
     xlab = "log10 body mass (kg)", ylab = "log10 brain mass (g)")
abline(fit)
pct <- 100 * (mammals$brain / 1000) / mammals$body   # brain as % of body mass
names(pct) <- rownames(mammals)
round(pct[c("Mouse", "Human", "African elephant")], 3)
```

a. What is the slope, to three decimals?
b. Does its 95 % confidence interval include 1? Does it include 2/3 (0.667)?
c. What percentage of body mass is brain in the mouse and in the African
   elephant?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
(Intercept) log10(body) 
      0.927       0.752 
            2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept) 0.844  1.011
log10(body) 0.695  0.809
           Mouse            Human African elephant 
           1.739            2.129            0.086 
```

a. **0.752**, so brain mass ∝ body mass^0.75.
b. **No and no.** The interval 0.695–0.809 excludes both 1 and 0.667. Brain
   mass rises less steeply than body mass, but more steeply than simple
   surface area; it is close to the 3/4 exponent often found for whole-body
   metabolic rate.
c. **Mouse 1.739 %, African elephant 0.086 %.** On a log–log plot a slope
   below 1 means that each organ makes up a smaller fraction of a larger body,
   just as surface area per unit volume falls when a cube gets bigger.
:::

### B5. Which mammal has the largest brain for its size?

The line from B4 predicts the brain mass expected for a given body mass. A
residual on the log₁₀ scale converts to a ratio: `10^residual` is observed
brain mass divided by expected brain mass. Run this after the code in B4.

```r
ratio <- 10^residuals(fit)                 # observed / expected brain mass
round(sort(ratio, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 1)
round(sort(ratio)[1:3], 2)
mammals[c("Human", "African elephant"), ]
```

a. Which species has the highest ratio, and how many times larger is its brain
   than expected for its body mass?
b. Which species has the lowest ratio?
c. Which species in the data has the heaviest brain in absolute terms?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
        Human Rhesus monkey        Baboon    Owl monkey    Chimpanzee 
          7.0           5.0           3.6           3.2           2.7 
Water opossum        Tenrec    Musk shrew 
         0.18          0.33          0.38 
                   body brain
Human              62  1320
African elephant 6654  5712
```

a. **Human, 7.0 times** the expected brain mass. The next four are also
   primates.
b. **Water opossum** (0.18 of expected).
c. **African elephant** (5712 g against 1320 g in humans). Absolute size and
   size relative to the scaling line answer different questions: only the
   second removes the effect of body size, which is why comparative
   physiologists compare residuals rather than raw values.
:::

### B6. The protein that makes connective tissue strong

Connective tissue is defined by its extracellular matrix. In tendon and bone
the main matrix protein is collagen type I. Search UniProtKB for
`gene:COL1A1 AND organism_id:9606 AND reviewed:true` and open the entry.

a. What is the accession?
b. In *Subcellular Location*, where does the protein end up?
c. In the *Features* table, between which positions is the
   "Triple-helical region"?
d. Run the code. In the triple-helical region, what fraction of the triplets
   (residues 1, 4, 7, … of the region) start with glycine (G)?

```r
lines <- readLines("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P02452.fasta")
col1  <- paste(lines[-1], collapse = "")
nchar(col1)                                   # whole precursor
helix <- substr(col1, 179, 1192)              # triple-helical region
aa    <- strsplit(helix, "")[[1]]
first <- aa[seq(1, length(aa), by = 3)]       # first residue of each triplet
length(first)
sum(first == "G")
round(100 * mean(aa == "G"), 1)               # % glycine in the helix
round(100 * mean(strsplit(col1, "")[[1]] == "G"), 1)   # % glycine overall
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] 1464
[1] 338
[1] 338
[1] 33.6
[1] 26.7
```

a. **P02452** (CO1A1_HUMAN, collagen alpha-1(I) chain).
b. It is **secreted into the extracellular matrix**; the *Tissue specificity*
   comment says it forms the fibrils of tendon, ligaments and bone.
c. **179–1192** (1014 residues, 338 triplets).
d. **All of them: 338 of 338.** Every third residue is glycine, the only amino
   acid small enough to sit in the centre of the triple helix. Glycine is
   33.6 % of the helix but only 26.7 % of the whole precursor, which also has
   a signal peptide and propeptides that are removed. A single glycine change
   in the helix can weaken the matrix; this is the cause of many cases of
   osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease), listed under the entry's
   *Disease & Variants* section.
:::
